q: Le Chatelier's principle was discovered by French Chemist Henri Louis Le Chatelier in 1884.
e: True. Le Chatelier's principle was discovered by French Chemist Henri Louis Le Chatelier in 1884. Le Chatelier says an equilibrium shifts to oppose a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature.

q: If a system is in equilibrium and when any of the factors affecting the chemical equilibrium is changed, the equilibrium shifts so as to enhance the effect of the change.
e: False. Le Chatelier says the system shifts to oppose the change, not to enhance it. It fights the stress.

q: Once equilibrium is established in a system, no further change is apparent as long as the external factors remain unchanged.
e: True. Once equilibrium is established in a system, no further change is apparent as long as the external factors remain unchanged. Equilibrium is when forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant.

q: The changes in concentration, temperature, and pressure of the system are external factors that affect equilibrium.
e: True. The changes in concentration, temperature, and pressure of the system are external factors that affect equilibrium. Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions.

q: In some cases, stress causes no shift in the equilibrium, especially when the moles of reactants and products are equal after the change in the pressure of gases.
e: True. In some cases, stress causes no shift in the equilibrium, especially when the moles of reactants and products are equal after the change in the pressure of gases. Equilibrium is when forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant.

q: Le Chatelier's principle describes how a chemical equilibrium shifts in response to a stress within an open system.
e: False. The principle is stated for a closed system at equilibrium. An open system may never hold a true chemical equilibrium.

q: A change in concentration, temperature, or pressure makes a difference in the amount of product formed in a reaction.
e: True. A change in concentration, temperature, or pressure makes a difference in the amount of product formed in a reaction. Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions.

q: A catalyst does not affect the equilibrium concentrations and there is no change in equilibrium.

q: Adding or removing a reactant or product from a reaction mixture at equilibrium will always disturb the equilibrium.
e: True. Adding or removing a reactant or product from a reaction mixture at equilibrium will always disturb the equilibrium. Equilibrium is when forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant.

q: When the concentration of a reactant is increased, the system responds by proceeding in the reverse direction in favour of reactants.
e: False. Extra reactant drives the forward reaction, making more product, until a new balance is reached. The reverse direction would add even more reactant.

q: When the concentration of a reactant is decreased, the system responds by adding the concentration of the reactant, thus the reaction proceeds in the reverse direction.
e: True. When the concentration of a reactant is decreased, the system responds by adding the concentration of the reactant, thus the reaction proceeds in the reverse direction. Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions.

q: When the concentration of a product is increased, the system responds by removing the concentration of the product, thus the reaction proceeds in the forward direction.
e: False. Extra product drives the reverse reaction. The system removes some product by going backward, not forward.

q: When the concentration of a product is decreased, the system responds by adding the concentration of the product, thus the reaction proceeds in the forward direction.
e: True. When the concentration of a product is decreased, the system responds by adding the concentration of the product, thus the reaction proceeds in the forward direction. Higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions.

q: The effect of temperature on chemical equilibrium depends upon the heat changes ($\Delta H$) of the reaction.
e: True. The effect of temperature on chemical equilibrium depends upon the heat changes (deltaH) of the reaction. Equilibrium is when forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant.

q: If a thermochemical equation is given, the value of heat change is for the reverse reaction.
e: False. The written delta H belongs to the reaction as written, the forward direction. Reverse the arrow and you reverse the sign.

q: A temperature decrease favours an exothermic reaction, and a temperature increase favours an endothermic reaction.
e: True. A temperature decrease favours an exothermic reaction, and a temperature increase favours an endothermic reaction. Endothermic means the system takes in heat, so delta H is positive.

q: In the case of exothermic reactions, decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic reaction by releasing heat.
e: True. In the case of exothermic reactions, decreasing the temperature favours the exothermic reaction by releasing heat. Higher temperature means a larger fraction of particles have energy at least Ea.

q: In the case of endothermic reactions, increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium towards the reverse reaction.
e: False. Heat is a reactant in an endothermic change, so extra temperature favours the forward reaction. The reverse would be exothermic.

q: The decomposition of $N_2O_4$ to $NO_2$ has a positive $\Delta H$, which means that the forward reaction is exothermic.
e: False. Positive delta H means the forward reaction is endothermic. N2O4 splitting to brown NO2 takes in heat.

q: When the temperature of the $N_2O_4$ and $NO_2$ equilibrium mixture is decreased, it favours the exothermic reaction and more $N_2O_4$ is obtained.

q: Pressure changes markedly affect the solid or liquid phases in a chemical equilibrium.
e: False. Pressure mainly affects equilibria that involve gases. Solids and liquids are almost incompressible, so their amounts barely shift with pressure.

q: The pressure of a gas mixture at a given temperature is determined by the number of gas molecules in a given volume.

q: If the pressure is increased, the position of equilibrium will shift towards the side with more moles of gas.

q: According to Le Chatelier's principle, as pressure decreases, the equilibrium moves toward the side of the reaction with more moles of gas.
e: True. According to Le Chatelier's principle, as pressure decreases, the equilibrium moves toward the side of the reaction with more moles of gas. Le Chatelier says an equilibrium shifts to oppose a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature.

q: If the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides of the reversible chemical equation, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right.
e: False. Equal gas moles means pressure does not shift the position. There is no fewer-moles side to run toward.

q: The synthesis of ammonia (Haber process) is a good example of an industrial process that uses Le Chatelier's principle.

q: In the synthesis of ammonia, the forward reaction is favoured at high temperatures because the reaction is exothermic.

q: The forward reaction in ammonia production is favoured by high pressure because there are four moles of reactants for every two moles of product formed.

q: Methanol is produced from carbon monoxide and hydrogen in an endothermic reaction.
